With curl's default User-Agent (no -A flag), same URL -> HTTP 200, 70,913 bytes, byte-for-byte the same size the 2026-09-16 researcher recorded. This is a THIRD independent reproduction of the same host-level quirk, each run surfacing a different curl exit code (researcher: 52 "Empty reply from server"; fact-checker: 92 "HTTP/2 stream INTERNAL_ERROR"; this run: 56) but always on investors.broadcom.com specifically and always resolved by dropping the custom UA on that one host. Confirmed genuine article body: matches, and Jalape/Celestica/Tomahawk/GLOBE NEWSWIRE/tape-out/Brockman/Hock Tan/Richard Ho/"may be the fastest"/"substantially better than current state-of-the-art"/"designed for initial deployment by the end of 2026"/"undue reliance" all present by direct grep. (2) https://investors.broadcom.com/news-releases/news-release-details/openai-and-broadcom-announce-strategic-collaboration-deploy-10 -> default UA -> HTTP 200, 71,384 bytes (again identical to both prior agents' byte counts). Confirmed genuine: title matches, "800 million weekly active users", "second half of 2026", "end of 2029", "term sheet", "Kawwas", "Altman" all present. (3) https://openai.com/index/openai-broadcom-jalapeno-inference-chip -> WITH "Mokaair-editorial" (no fallback needed) -> 1 redirect to the canonical .../jalapeno-inference-chip/ (trailing slash), HTTP 200, 403,576-403,585 bytes (two fetches a few minutes apart varied by ~9 bytes, immaterial). This is the FIRST successful read of OpenAI's own post in this article's research history; both 2026-09-16 passes got HTTP 403 with a ~9.8 KB Cloudflare body on this exact URL and its variants. Sites' bot-protection configurations are not static; today's fetch is genuine, not a fluke of URL guessing (the URL itself is unchanged from what the official RSS feed printed on 2026-09-16). The page is a Next.js app-router page: the readable prose is not in the initial HTML as plain <p> text but inside `self.__next_f.push([1,"..."])` RSC-stream chunks, each a JSON-encoded string. Extracted with a small Python script that bracket-matches each push(...) call and json.loads()s the array, then filtered the resulting quoted strings for prose (>=35 chars, >=5 spaces, >=25 letters, not a URL/className). This produced 72 candidate strings that included the full article body, all four section headings, all three quotes, and the meta description/og:description. Cross-checked every sentence used in the article against this extraction before writing verbatim_quote fields below. The RSS feed (openai.com/news/rss.xml) was NOT re-fetched and is NOT in sources[], per corrections-ai.md source_list_fix #1 (two Broadcom pages already meet the 2-4 minimum, and BRIEF says sources holds article-page URLs, not feed URLs); this also removes the need to carry the four feed-only facts (exact RSS <item> pubDate/description, and the two 2026-08-25 follow-up post titles) that the prior research record leaned on — none of those four are used as article evidence here. editorial_brief: READER: a Taiwanese general reader who uses ChatGPT or a similar assistant and has no hardware background. Question answered: 'why does the company that makes the model now make the chip, and what does that change for me?' — not 'is this chip good'. ANGLE: an AI service is a stack (product, model, serving system, chip); on 2026-06-24 OpenAI and Broadcom showed the bottom layer of that stack for the first time, and the interesting part is what an announcement at this stage can and cannot tell you. SPINE: the gap between announcement and availability — a chip that has taped out and is running in a lab on engineering samples, a deployment 'designed for' the end of 2026, a performance report promised 'in the coming months', and a formal forward-looking-statements notice attached by Broadcom itself. FIVE SECTIONS: (1) what was announced and in whose words, noting the two companies' own headlines differ; (2) who did which part — OpenAI the architecture, Broadcom the silicon and Tomahawk networking, Celestica the board/rack/system (uncorroborated by Celestica itself) — table here; (3) what stage it is actually at: nine months to tape-out (not production, and the two companies even hedge the 'fastest ever' claim differently from each other), engineering samples running GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark, no measured numbers — diagram here; (4) deployment: gigawatt scale, end of 2026, Microsoft named, the forward-looking-statement caveat, and the separate, earlier 2025-10-13 10 GW collaboration kept distinct; (5) how to read a chip announcement — observed fact vs vendor claim vs forward-looking statement, including the conditional industry-wide cost sentence that both companies' own pages carry (not a Jalapeño-specific savings figure). TONE: only figures that appear in the body are used in the table/diagram: 2026-06-24, nine months, end of 2026, 2025-10-13, 100 億瓦/10 gigawatts (attached to the 2025 announcement only), second half of 2026 and end of 2029 (2025 announcement only), and over 800 million weekly active users (2025-10-13 only, always dated). DELIBERATELY OUT OF SCOPE: whether this threatens NVIDIA, Broadcom's or OpenAI's finances, chip-industry supply-chain politics, Taiwanese suppliers, any judgement on whether custom silicon is the right strategy.
